sentences.text: The genus name Aetodactylus means "eagle finger" and it belongs to the Targaryendraconia group of pterosaurs.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — lower jaw measures 38.4 cm in total length, with the symphysis accounting for 15.8 cm.
The fossil preserves evidence of 27 pairs of teeth, described as pointed, slightly curved backward, flattened, and slender.
Unlike related genera like Anhanguera and Ornithocheirus, Aetodactylus lacks a bony crest on its lower jaw.
Aetodactylus is notable for being one of the youngest definitive records of the ornithocheirid family.
The holotype specimen was discovered in 2006 by Lance Hall near a construction site in Mansfield, Texas.
Timothy S. Myers named the genus Aetodactylus in 2010, and the type species A. halli was named to honor the discoverer, Lance Hall.
Aetodactylus is distinguished from other ornithocheirids by features such as an expanded anterior jaw, a strongly compressed symphysis, evenly spaced teeth, and an upward curve of the lower jaw.
While originally thought to be related to Boreopterus, later analysis placed Aetodactylus closely related to Cimoliopterus.
Aetodactylus represents one of the earliest known ornithocheirids.
Fossils of Aetodactylus were found in the Tarrant Formation, a marine sandstone dating to approximately 97 million years ago during the middle Cenomanian.
Aetodactylus lived approximately 98 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in what is now the United States.
The time range for Aetodactylus is estimated between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.
